did_you_know.text: Did you know? Mordecai responded to the decree of destruction by mourning publicly: he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the city, crying out loudly and bitterly.
Did you know? Although Mordecai went as far as the king’s gate, he did not enter it, because according to local custom, no one was allowed to enter the king’s gate wearing sackcloth.
Did you know? Mordecai was not the only one mourning: throughout all the king’s provinces, the Jews fasted, wept, and mourned, and many put on sackcloth and ashes.
Did you know? Esther tried to replace Mordecai’s mourning clothes with ordinary garments, but he refused to accept them; this caused her great alarm.
Did you know? Esther sent Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs appointed to attend her, to find out why Mordecai was mourning and what had happened.

Did you know? Mordecai also gave Hathach a copy of the written decree issued in Susa, so that Esther could see the order and understand that she needed to appeal to the king for mercy on behalf of her people.

Did you know? Esther explained that entering the king’s inner court without being summoned could result in death, unless the king extended his golden scepter. She also noted that she had not been summoned to the king for thirty days.
Did you know? Mordecai warned Esther not to assume that living in the palace would protect her, and suggested that perhaps she had become queen precisely to act at this critical moment.
Did you know? Esther did not act alone: she asked all the Jews of Susa to fast for three days, and she and her attendants fasted as well before she entered the king’s presence without being summoned.
Did you know? After Esther made her decision, Mordecai did everything she had commanded him to do, bringing the chapter to a close with a transition from warnings to united action.
